Field surveys of Pronodularia japanensis in Japanese river systems have provided detailed information on its early life-history traits. Newly released glochidia, the parasitic larval stage, exhibit a shell length at birth of 0.02 centimeters [Lb = 0.02 centimeters], a minute size that facilitates attachment to host fish gills. After a period of parasitic encystment, the larvae undergo metamorphosis and subsequently settle onto the substrate as exogenously feeding juveniles. At the moment of settlement, these recently metamorphosed individuals possess a shell length of 0.03 centimeters , marking the transition to a benthic, filter-feeding existence. These diminutive dimensions at the onset of the free-living stage are typical of unionid mussels and reflect the substantial energetic investment required for the post-parasitic transformation and the establishment of a functional feeding apparatus in the juvenile spat.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the embryonic development of Pronodularia japanensis proceeds rapidly. The age at birth, defined as the moment of glochidial release from the marsupial gills of the adult female, is approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days] at a temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. This abbreviated brooding period is a defining feature of the species and stands in contrast to the protracted incubation durations observed in many marine bivalves. The thermal regime of 22 °C [T = 22 °C] is representative of late spring and early summer water temperatures in its native lotic habitats, thus ensuring that glochidial release coincides with the peak activity of suitable fish hosts. The timing of this release is a critical life-history event, as glochidia must encounter a compatible host within a very short window to complete their development.

The life-history trajectory of Pronodularia japanensis continues with a prolonged period of somatic growth and eventual reproductive maturation. Puberty, defined as the onset of gonadal activity and the capacity for gamete production, is attained when an individual reaches a shell length of 3.0 centimeters [Lp = 3.0 centimeters], a threshold that, when compared to the ultimate shell length of 5.5 centimeters [Li = 5.5 centimeters], indicates that a considerable portion of the lifespan is dedicated to growth beyond the reproductive onset. This substantial size difference between maturity and the final attainable shell length may allow for exponential increases in fecundity with increasing body size, a pattern common among bivalves.

For a species with an extended reproductive lifespan, the maximum rate of reproductive output is a key demographic parameter. For Pronodularia japanensis, the daily reproductive rate at 22 °C [T = 22 °C] is expressed through a combination of brood size and spawning frequency. Females produce approximately 438 offspring per day [Ri = approximately 438 offspring per day], with a single, synchronized release event each year [F_R_i = single, synchronized release event each year]. This high daily fecundity, which reflects the volumetric constraints of the marsupial gill chamber, is balanced against the low spawning frequency, and the annual cycle is tightly coupled to the seasonal abundance of host fish and thermal requirements for successful larval development.

An assessment of adult body condition provides a link between somatic investment and reproductive potential. At a shell length of 5.1 centimeters, which is close to the species' maximum recorded size, the total wet weight of an individual Pronodularia japanensis is approximately 14.4 grams [Wwi = approximately 14.4 grams]. This mass reflects the accumulation of soft tissues and shell material necessary to sustain high metabolic demands and support gravidity. Furthermore, the maximum lifespan of Pronodularia japanensis in stable habitats at 22 °C [T = 22 °C] is remarkable, with the oldest documented individuals attaining an age of approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years]. This longevity is a common trait among unionid mussels and allows for repeated reproductive contributions across multiple seasons, thereby buffering the population against years of poor recruitment.
